identity: Specific lift-ground etching procedure, distinguished from the pinned scratched-ground etching identity by how areas become exposed. Scope idea and aliases fit the source.
qualifications: The discovery card leaves subsequent treatment open. The takeaway should say aquatint is optional/often used, because the source does not require it.
claims: Soluble drawing and overlying resistant ground are removed selectively by water
Sugar lift entry 97–98 gives the complete preparation sequence.
Exposed drawing determines later acid etching; aquatint can precede it
Etching is explicit; aquatint is described as often used, not necessary. The takeaway omits that distinction.
supported_with_qualification_correction
relations: Princeton directly calls sugar lift a lift-ground technique that exposes drawn regions to acid etching; the pinned target is specifically printmaking etching, not another sense of etching.

missing_parent_links.note: An optional more informative parent link is defensible: source identifies this as an etching technique. Current related_to is true but less specific. This is an advisory, not a mandatory hierarchy.

findings.finding: The source makes aquatint optional, whereas the takeaway’s combined aquatint-and-etching sequence can sound obligatory.

correction: Change takeaway to expose areas for etching, often after aquatint. The 43-word card itself is supported.

identity: Named Dutch reclaimed-lake landscape, distinct from the general polder type and the broad cultural-landscape control. A named_subject at idea scope is appropriate.
qualifications: Keeps the focus on a documented landscape; does not turn geometric organization into a universal polder rule.
claims: Reclaimed lakebed has a geometric pattern of fields, roads, canals and settlements
Brief synthesis 51–55 directly documents reclamation and the grid.
Design aims and water/agricultural management jointly shape the place
Flood control, new agricultural land and Renaissance planning are all explicit; final sentence is a faithful explanatory synthesis.
relations: UNESCO identifies Beemster as a polder created by draining a lake and managing dykes/canals. Its relationship to the general polder-landscape target is direct.

identity: A bounded archaeological application of stratigraphy. The pinned Q134783 is geological layering, while this card applies layer order to human deposits; facet_or_application is supported.
qualifications: The undisturbed-deposit condition and generally wording are retained. Rearrangement warning follows directly from that condition.
claims: Layer sequences support relative ordering of archaeological activity
Dating-methods context and Stratigraphy row explicitly link deposits to relative age.
Lower precedes upper only in an undisturbed sequence
The source expressly conditions superposition on lack of disturbance.
relations: Application_of the pinned geological-layering meaning is a reasonable disciplinary bridge; it is correctly marked editorial rather than claiming the NPS passage explicitly names Wikidata’s general concept.

identity: One identified Benin brass plaque, accession 1978.412.309, distinct from generic hierarchical scale. Named-subject and narrow scope are supported by collection details.
qualifications: Political-rank reading is the museum’s explicit interpretation, not inferred merely from visible size.
claims: A mounted ruler and attendants occur on a Benin palace brass plaque
Collection description 10–11 and object details 57–66 establish the work, medium and court setting.
Relative size expresses rank
The museum explicitly names hierarchical scale and its rank function.
relations: The cited passage directly connects this exact plaque with hierarchical scale. The target denotes rank-encoding relative size and resolves in the frozen batch.

identity: Illusionistic object-presence effect, distinct from anamorphic viewpoint distortion and from the baseline faux-material painting sense.
qualifications: Uses aims and possibility, so no guarantee that a viewer will be deceived. The image/object distinction is explanatory paraphrase.
claims: Trompe-l’oeil can make a painting look like the depicted object itself
National Gallery definition 125–126 directly supports the intended deception.
It concerns apparent object presence, rather than realism alone
The source’s object-versus-painting distinction supports this careful elaboration.
relations: The comparison with anamorphosis is expressly editorial; a12 supplies deceptive presence and a13 explicitly supplies viewpoint-resolved distortion. It is not mislabeled equivalence or parenthood.

identity: Community concept in Buddhism, distinct from Buddhism as a broad field and Pratimoksha as a code governing part of the community.
qualifications: Sometimes, can, and context preserve variation in whether lay followers are included; no universal claim about every community.
claims: Sangha can mean ordained community or a broader body including laity
Summary 145 and paragraph 149 distinguish these uses.
Teaching/guidance and material support sustain reciprocal relations
Paragraph 152 explicitly describes both directions of support.
relations: Paragraph 151 actually names Pratimoksha and connects it to the ordained members of the community. This supports the specific relationship, not merely two independent Buddhist facts.

identity: Denominator-based preparation facet for choropleth data, distinct from the map form itself and from the broad Cartography control.
qualifications: A relevant denominator is required; the card does not promise that normalization removes all visual or statistical bias.
claims: Normalization divides a count by a relevant total
Lines 68 and 111 define denominator choice and division.
Per-person comparison answers a different question from totals
Lines 102–112 contrast raw restaurant counts with per-capita patterns; cases per resident is an explicitly illustrative analogous example.
relations: The documentation directly instructs normalization when creating choropleth maps, supporting facet_of this map form.

identity: A specific interview-context recording practice within Oral history, not a duplicate of the whole method or narrator-review facet.
qualifications: Appropriate pseudonyms and generic home-setting wording preserve the source’s privacy qualification.
claims: Lead-in supplies who, full date, setting and intended subject at each session’s start
Interviewing item 2 enumerates these contextual identifiers.
Avoid unnecessary exposure of a private residence address
Item 2 explicitly recommends a generic home description instead of address.
relations: The practice appears as a numbered interviewing step in the OHA’s oral-history best practices, directly supporting facet_of the resolved Oral history target.

identity: The compositional idea is distinguishable from general figure–ground perception. The linked work resolves by object URL, but its title/date metadata and drawing medium wording need correction.
qualifications: Negative-space mechanism is supported. Treat the object as the identified 1965 lithograph; the museum’s gallery prose says drawings, but the structured object header/medium are unambiguous.
claims: Unmarked spaces help articulate forms in Asawa’s Chair
Gallery label 78–79 explicitly describes additional chairs within negative space.
The cited object is a drawing with c.1963 source-title metadata
Header 61–68 and medium 88 identify Chair (TAM.1558-II), 1965, Lithograph. The source title and drawing wording should be corrected.
unsupported_object_description
relations: Actual use of negative space in the specific linked Chair object is explicitly supported by the gallery label. The relation remains valid after its note is corrected from drawing to work/lithograph and the target’s matching medium wording is repaired.

findings.finding: The exact object is the 1965 lithograph Chair (TAM.1558-II); a09’s c.1963 title and both cards’ drawing descriptions misdescribe it. The negative-space claim and conceptual relationship are supported.

correction: Correct a09 title to the verified work title/date. Replace drawing references in sampled takeaway/relation and unsampled Chair target with work or lithograph; extend evidence locators to object header and medium. Preserve IDs and sample membership, increment affected versions, and recheck.

identity: Holbein’s named double portrait, not the abstract anamorphosis technique or another work sharing the title. URL and source identify the work.
qualifications: The special viewpoint is preserved; no claim that every object or the whole portrait becomes legible only obliquely.
claims: Two sitters and depicted objects surround a distorted skull
Overview 102–104 and in-depth account establish composition.
An oblique lower-right view resolves the skull
Lines 122–123 explicitly describe the viewing position and named technique.
relations: The gallery explicitly calls the skull effect anamorphosis. The exact work-to-technique connection supports source_asserted related_to.

identity: General doorway scroll/practice rather than the specific Ilya Schor museum object or just its decorative case. The museum label supplies a general definition.
qualifications: Usually within a case leaves room for practice variation; does not imply the case alone fulfills the textual practice.
claims: Parchment inscribed with Torah verses is attached at a doorway
Label 39–40 explicitly identifies Torah inscription and doorpost use.
The written scroll underlies the practice, with a protective case
The definition is the scroll; protective enclosure and placement follow.
relations: The text explicitly identifies the inscription as Torah verses, exactly matching the pinned first-five-books meaning of Q34990.

identity: Narrator reflection on telling, separate from metafiction and baseline narrative metalepsis. Narrow idea scope is justified.
qualifications: Need not announce fictionality and may organize narration preserve the source’s distinction and non-exclusivity.
claims: Metanarration concerns the act/process of telling
Definition 46–47 directly distinguishes it from fictional-status commentary.
It can organize communication and occur in nonfiction
Explication 55–59 explicitly covers nonfiction and directing/communicative functions.
relations: The source explicitly says the two concepts are related but distinct and explains their different objects of reflection. The link is supported as related_to, not equivalence.

identity: Christian scriptural typology, expressly distinct from archaeological artifact typology and from canon membership.
qualifications: Catholic teaching is attributed. The card retains Old Testament intrinsic value and does not present doctrinal truth as an unqualified secular fact.
claims: Earlier scriptural events are read as prefigurations of later fulfillment
Catechism 128 describes the Old Covenant/Christ typological relation.
This does not erase the earlier texts’ value in Catholic teaching
Paragraphs 129–130 explicitly preserve that intrinsic value.
relations: Connection to canon as a bounded collection is labeled editorial; the source’s two-Testament interpretive setting provides the factual premise without claiming the canon concept is identical to typology.

identity: Named class of shrine tablets used in domestic veneration, distinct from omamori portable amulets and from Shinto generally.
qualifications: Sacred protection is explicitly attributed to practitioners’ understanding rather than asserted as a causal fact.
claims: Ofuda bear kami or shrine names on paper/wood and go on home altars
Ofuda paragraph 15 explicitly describes materials, inscriptions and usual location.
They carry an attributed protective connection to the shrine
Opening 4 and paragraph 15 describe kami presence/power and family protection.
relations: The source directly situates ofuda in shrine/kami domestic practice, which is the pinned Shinto meaning; r21 independently confirms jinja as Shinto sites. Current source assertion is defensible; adding r21 would make the named broad target especially explicit.

identity: Bounded western Christian tradition, distinct from Christianity as a whole and from one particular monastic rule.
qualifications: Could and did not necessarily avoid treating all communities as identical. Historical social services and arts claims are supported by a medieval source.
claims: Disciplined withdrawal took solitary and communal forms
Paragraphs 185–188 contrast eremitic and cenobitic possibilities.
Communities could support travelers, learning and artistic work
Paragraphs 189–190 directly describe hospitality, education and art, supporting the withdrawal/social-connection distinction.
relations: Paragraphs 194–197 explicitly connect Benedict’s rule with widespread western communal monastic life.

missing_parent_links.note: A Christianity parent is defensible from the Christian-monastic discussion and pinned identity. Current relation to the rule is valid; record the optional missing broader link without imposing a four-level tree.

identity: Creator-established internal sequence, distinct from creator-origin grouping under archival provenance; the two related principles are not duplicates.
qualifications: When meaningful and can preserve the source’s non-absolute treatment of original order.
claims: Original order concerns a creator’s record organization and sequence
Definition 19 establishes origin of the arrangement.
Retaining meaningful order preserves evidential/functional connections
Schellenberg 22 says order may reveal significance; provenance discussion explains creator-purpose relationships.
relations: The editorial comparison correctly distinguishes internal arrangement from provenance grouping. SAA additionally cross-references them and explicitly describes original order as a component of provenance.

identity: Named artist’s documented role and practice, distinct from the movement’s optical-mixing concept and broad color theory.
qualifications: The card does not assert optical mixing as a proven physical mechanism; the relationship’s target preserves the artists’ theoretical aim.
claims: Signac promoted Neo-Impressionism through practice and writing after Seurat
Lines 90–91 explicitly document the role and treatise.
Watercolors extended his exploration of color
Line 92 directly describes purity/clarity investigation in that medium.
relations: Lines 81–82 explicitly associate Signac with the separated-color optical-mixture theory; this is direct support, beyond the more general fact he belonged to the movement.

identity: Equal-feature-count classification, distinct from equal-width interval classification and from dataset-cluster breaks. Application/facet scope fits map design.
qualifications: Roughly equal accommodates practical grouping and the card retains both misleading grouping caveats.
claims: Quantile puts similar numbers of features in classes
Quantile paragraph 15 states the count-based rule.
Near values may split while far values may share classes
Paragraph 16 explicitly states both caveats.
relations: The source’s data-classification section explicitly lists quantile and equal interval as alternative numerical mapping methods and spells out their contrasting rules; no parent/equivalence is inferred.
The link to Cartography is expressly editorial and supported by the source’s map-symbolization purpose and the pinned map-design meaning.

identity: Occurrence-to-telling frequency relation, distinct from iterative and repetitive narration and from broad literature. Not a duration category.
qualifications: The long-account example is a logical illustration of the source’s separate frequency and duration dimensions, not a claimed historical text example.
claims: Singulative tells one occurrence once
Frequency paragraph 90 directly gives the definition.
Passage length does not itself define frequency
Lines 88–90 separate duration categories from occurrence/telling counts.
relations: The same paragraph explicitly contrasts singulative with iterative frequency, supporting source_asserted related_to.

identity: Swift’s named satirical novel, distinct from a generic travel genre and Bradbury’s later work.
qualifications: The critical explanation is directly the NEA guide’s reading; card does not claim distant-world satire originated with Swift.
claims: Invented journeys reflect flaws recognizable in Swift’s society
Literary Allusions 43–44 explicitly interprets fanciful islands as social mirrors.
Satire provides more than fantastic adventure
The source labels the novel satirical and articulates its social function.
relations: NEA directly compares this distant-world mirror strategy to Fahrenheit 451. Actual work-to-work relation is explicit, not just co-appearance on a reading list.
